title: The family of Tietz potentials
abstract: We show that several potential-energy functions based on the exponential function $e^{-αr}$, $α> 0$, are either equivalent or identical to the Tietz potential. Some of those potentials exhibit redundant parameters that can be removed without affecting their performance for the description of the vibration-rotation spectra of diatomic molecules.
summary: This paper investigates the mathematical relationships between various potential energy functions used to model diatomic molecules. The authors prove that many different functional forms, including the Tietz potential, are either identical or equivalent to each other. This suggests that for describing molecular spectra, many complex potentials are mathematically redundant.
main_problem: To demonstrate that various potential-energy functions, particularly those based on the exponential function, are mathematically equivalent or identical to the established Tietz potential.
main_result: Many complex potentials used in molecular physics reduce to the form of the Tietz potential, suggesting that different functional forms are physically redundant for describing vibration-rotation spectra.
method: The analysis uses the concept of potential equivalence, defined by the equality of the derivative of the potentials, and compares various functional forms against the standard Tietz potential.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the potential energy functions V(r) used in the Hamiltonian H = T + V(r) to model the vibration-rotation spectra of diatomic molecules.
key_observables: Vibration-rotation spectra, potential energy functions V(r).
important_parameters: The equilibrium distance ($r_e$) and the dissociation energy ($D_e$) are crucial parameters used to normalize and compare the potentials.
main_assumptions: Equivalence between potentials is defined by the equality of their derivatives, which implies sharing the same eigenfunctions for the Hamiltonian.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares numerous potential forms (e.g., Hua, FPEP, DFPEP, etc.) against the Tietz potential, demonstrating their mathematical relationships and parameter redundancies.
why_interesting: This work directly impacts the theoretical modeling of molecular spectroscopy by showing that a vast array of complex potentials can be unified into a single, simpler functional form, simplifying theoretical treatments.
